lesson.title: How Much Fits in the Pipe: The Bandwidth Delay Product
lesson.summary: The bandwidth delay product multiplies a link's bandwidth by its round trip time to reveal how much data can be in flight at once, a number that determines whether a protocol's window size can actually use the link's full speed.
lesson.body:
The bandwidth delay product, often abbreviated BDP, is the amount of data that can be in transit on a network path at any given instant, calculated by multiplying the link's bandwidth by the round trip time. Both quantities are ones covered earlier in this sequence: bandwidth describes how many bits per second a link can carry, and RTT describes how long a round trip takes on that path. Multiplying them together converts a rate and a time into an amount of data.

A useful way to picture this is a pipe. Bandwidth is like the pipe's width, determining how much water can flow through it per second. Propagation delay, and by extension RTT, is like the pipe's length, determining how long a given drop of water spends inside the pipe before coming out the other end. The bandwidth delay product is then the total volume of water that fits inside the pipe at once, the amount that is in flight, neither yet delivered nor yet acknowledged.

As a concrete example, take a link with 100 Mbps of bandwidth and an RTT of 80 milliseconds. Converting to consistent units, bandwidth is 100,000,000 bits per second and RTT is 0.080 seconds. Multiplying gives 8,000,000 bits, which is 1,000,000 bytes, or roughly 976.6 kibibytes, of data that can be in flight on this path at any moment if the link is to be kept fully busy.

This number matters enormously for protocols like TCP, which only sends a limited amount of unacknowledged data at a time, controlled by its window size. If a TCP connection's window is smaller than the path's bandwidth delay product, the sender will run out of data it is allowed to send and sit idle waiting for acknowledgments to return, even though the link itself has spare capacity. The original TCP window field allows a maximum of 65,535 bytes, only about 6.5 percent of the 1,000,000 byte bandwidth delay product in the example above, which would badly underutilize that link. This is exactly why TCP window scaling, defined in RFC 1323, was introduced: it lets a connection negotiate a much larger effective window, sized appropriately for high bandwidth delay product paths.

Paths with a large bandwidth delay product are sometimes called long fat networks, a nod to both a long delay and a fat, high capacity pipe. Satellite links are a classic example, combining generous bandwidth with the roughly 500 millisecond RTT typical of geostationary orbit, and transcontinental fiber routes with high bandwidth and RTTs of 100 milliseconds or more show the same pattern. Any path where either bandwidth or RTT is unusually high deserves a bandwidth delay product calculation before assuming default protocol settings will use the link efficiently.

Bandwidth delay product is a good example of how the individual concepts in this chapter sequence combine into something practically useful. Bandwidth alone tells you a link's raw speed, and RTT alone tells you how long a round trip takes, but neither one by itself tells a protocol designer how large a buffer or window needs to be to actually use that speed over that distance. Only the product of the two answers that question.
